questions: Do you work or are you a student?
Why did you choose that job or subject?
What is a typical day like for you?
What do you find most challenging about your work or studies?
Would you like to change anything about your job or course?
Do you prefer working alone or with other people?
tips: Choose either work or study and stay consistent. You do not need to explain your whole career history.
Use present simple for routines and present continuous for temporary situations ('I'm currently doing an internship').
If you are unemployed or between jobs, say so honestly and talk about what you are doing now.
usefulPhrases: At the moment I'm in my final year of...
I ended up choosing it because...
A typical day kicks off with...
It can be quite demanding at times.
If I could change one thing, it would be...
I'd say I'm more of a team player.

samples.text:
[Do you work or are you a student?]
I am working now. I work in a bank as customer service, so my job is to help the customer when they have problem with their account or they want to open new account.

[Why did you choose that job?]
Actually, I study accounting in university, so I think bank is suitable for me. Also the salary is good and, um, my parents also want me to work in the bank because it is a stable job.

[What do you find most challenging about your work?]
The most challenging is when the customer is angry. Sometimes they are angry because the system is error and it is not my fault, but I must still be polite and smile. It is very tiring, especially when many customer come at the same time.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: the candidate answers each question at length and is willing to speak, but linking is mechanical ('also' is used repeatedly) and ideas are not always well sequenced. Lexical Resource: sufficient for the topic ('stable job', 'customer service'), though some word forms are wrong ('the system is error'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy: simple structures dominate, with frequent article and plural omissions ('have problem', 'many customer'); a few complex sentences are attempted successfully. Pronunciation: the hesitation marker 'um' and short clause units suggest a generally clear but somewhat flat delivery.

samples.text:
[Do you work or are you a student?]
I work full-time at a bank. I'm in customer service, so I deal with anything from people who've forgotten their PIN to small businesses wanting to open a loan account.

[Why did you choose that job?]
To be honest, it was partly practical. I'd studied accounting, so banking seemed like a natural fit, and it's a fairly secure job, which my parents were quite keen on. But I've found I actually enjoy the people side of it more than I expected.

[What do you find most challenging about your work?]
Definitely handling frustrated customers. Often the problem is something technical that I can't fix on the spot, so the challenge is keeping them calm while I find someone who can. It takes a lot of patience, especially on Mondays, when it's always packed.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: speaks at length without effort, using a range of connectives and discourse markers ('To be honest', 'But', 'Definitely') to organise ideas. Lexical Resource: flexible and accurate, with idiomatic chunks such as 'a natural fit', 'on the spot', 'the people side of it'. Grammatical Range & Accuracy: complex sentences with relative clauses and past perfect ('I'd studied') are produced accurately; errors are rare. Pronunciation: phrases like 'anything from... to...' suggest controlled chunking and intonation, although the transcript shows less variety in emphasis than a band 8 speaker would use.

samples.text:
[Why did you choose that job?]
If I'm completely honest, it was a pragmatic decision at first. I had an accounting degree and banking felt like the obvious route, plus my parents were very reassured by the idea of a secure position. What I didn't anticipate was how much I'd enjoy the interpersonal side, which has turned out to be the most rewarding part.

[What do you find most challenging about your work?]
Managing people's expectations, mainly. Customers often come in assuming I can override the system, and I have to explain, without sounding dismissive, that some things simply have to go through head office. Striking that balance between being sympathetic and being realistic takes a fair bit of tact.

[Do you prefer working alone or with other people?]
I'd say I thrive on a bit of both. I like bouncing ideas off colleagues, but when I'm reconciling accounts at the end of the day, I really need to shut myself away and concentrate.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: answers are developed coherently and effortlessly, with any hesitation sounding content-related rather than linguistic. Lexical Resource: wide, precise vocabulary used with ease ('pragmatic decision', 'override the system', 'striking that balance', 'bouncing ideas off colleagues'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy: a variety of structures, including cleft sentences ('What I didn't anticipate was...') and embedded clauses, all handled accurately. Pronunciation: the phrasing implies natural chunking and the use of stress to contrast ideas ('sympathetic and... realistic'), so the speaker would be easy to follow throughout.
